blocks.text: härdad - a Swedish tutor hardened all the way down

blocks.html: A conversational Swedish‑language tutor powered by Anthropic Claude. The application is the vehicle - the interesting part is everything attached to the image: signed evidence about how it was built, what's in it, and who vouches for it.

blocks.text: Started with python:3.13-slim. Measured what came with it

blocks.html: Before anything could claim to be hardened, I needed a baseline. Same FastAPI app, built on python:3.13-slim - the canonical community base. No opinions layered on top. This is the measurement against which every later change was compared.

Zero Critical, zero High - deceptively clean. The baseline's Python binaries aren't indexed as a scannable package, so upstream CPython CVEs don't surface against them. Visibility is part of what the next slide buys.
Same Python dependency closure, byte‑for‑byte. Only the base layer changed: from python:3.13-slim to dhi.io/python:3.13.

The Critical + High caveat. Both images ship CPython 3.13.13. The hardened scan surfaces 1 Critical (CVE-2026-6100) and 1 High (CVE-2026-4786) against the Python runtime - both freshly disclosed, currently not fixed upstream. The baseline's Python isn't mapped to these advisories; whether the same code paths are vulnerable is a separate question

Docker's 7‑day DHI patch SLA commits to shipping a rebuilt image within a week of a Critical/High fix landing upstream. "Not fixed" in a DHI scan has a tight, contractual resolution window; the community image has no equivalent guarantee.

Both images ship the identical FastAPI app and the same 36‑package Python dependency closure. Every node below the application root belongs to the base layer - that's what changed between them. The visual footprint is the attack surface.
Each panel scrolls independently. The two SVGs render at the same scale - scrollbar thumb length is a direct read on relative bloat. Rendered from the build‑time SPDX SBOMs in docs/sbom/ via mermaid.
Evidence attached to the image, not about it

Post‑hoc SBOMs (scanners) read /var/lib/dpkg/status after the fact. Build‑time attestations are emitted during the build by the system that knows exactly what it installed, then signed and recorded as sibling OCI artifacts anchored in Sigstore's Rekor transparency log.

No long‑lived private key. cosign keyless inverts the PGP/SSH model: you're not trusted because you hold a secret, you're trusted because Fulcio observed your OIDC authentication and recorded that observation publicly.

blocks.alt: Browser page confirming sigstore OIDC authentication succeeded
blocks.caption: cosign opens a browser → Fulcio verifies OIDC → short-lived cert issued → sign by digest. No key material ever touched the laptop.

blocks.text: From laptop build to GitHub Actions: L1 → L2

blocks.html: Attestations are only as trustworthy as the environment that produced them. Early builds ran on my laptop - real cosign signatures, real SBOM attestations, but a hostile observer has no way to tell whether I ran the declared build steps or quietly swapped them for others. Moving the build to GitHub Actions gave the attestations a custodian that isn't me.

items.title: Hardened build platform · isolated env, unreachable keys
items.desc: Defeats a malicious build step forging provenance · requires slsa-github-generator or equivalent, out of scope here

blocks.html: SLSA is per-artifact, not contagious. Building an L2 image FROM an L3 DHI base doesn't drag the base down to L2. Each layer's attestations are independently verifiable; a consumer can trace the DHI base to Docker's L3 provenance, and this image to its own L2 provenance, and trust each accordingly.
Workflow source: github.com/LennartOnGit/hardad/.github/workflows/docker-ci.yml buildx with provenance: mode=max, cosign sign-by-digest under GitHub OIDC, Scout policy gate.

blocks.text: Three out of four passing. Honestly.

blocks.html: The "only hardened base images" policy returns no data because Scout's base‑image detection can't trace through multi‑stage COPYs to identify DHI lineage. Honest talking point: "I use DHI but the automated detection couldn't verify it - in production I'd configure an exception or adjust the detection."

blocks.text: k3s · Helm · Apache reverse proxy · NodePort.

blocks.html: Bitnami PostgreSQL chart in a tutor namespace. Custom Helm chart for the app: 2 replicas, values.yaml + Kubernetes Secrets split, liveness/readiness probes, NodePort Service. Apache proxies /docker_demo to 192.168.177.30:30080.

blocks.text: What I haven't done, and how I'd frame it.

rows.text: Single‑node k3s only. Understand Deployments, Services, Helm, probes, Secrets. Haven't operated RBAC / network policies / production monitoring at scale.
Bypassed Traefik due to port‑80 conflict with Apache. Used NodePort + Apache proxy. Concept understood; rules not configured in practice.
Planned as Phase 3 (Sigstore Policy Controller). Trust model understood, not yet implemented.
Local arm64 builds deploy to the arm64 k3s cluster. CI produces amd64 for signing/policy demos. QEMU emulation is a known two‑line addition.
Phase 2. Infrastructure ready - Whisper (Mac‑native, MLX) + Piper TTS (sv_SE‑nst‑medium) reachable over LAN.

blocks.text: I deploy platforms before applying for the role.

Not slogans - tools I've used, errors I've debugged, and trade‑offs I can articulate. The full chain: Dockerfile, Kubernetes, CI pipeline, reverse proxy, database, application code. Signed, attested, policy‑gated, publicly deployed.
